summary:
Central Luzon stands under the national framework of the Philippines. The region enacts no criminal or civil code of its own on gender identity, and the national position on legal recognition, anti-discrimination coverage and detention conditions applies to a trans visitor here without regional modification.

Bataan is the one province in the region recorded as having a SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinance. The inventory does not record the ordinance's scope, its penalties, or any enforcement action taken under it, so what it changes in practice for a trans visitor or resident in Bataan is unresolved.

No trans-specific killing, assault, prosecution, refusal of service or official action in Central Luzon appears in the source inventory. The region's trans-relevant risk therefore rests on the national layer rather than on any documented regional pattern.
tangentialFactors:
Angeles City in Pampanga is the region's documented centre of commercial sexual exploitation and of anti-trafficking enforcement. The National Bureau of Investigation's Bataan District Office arrested the registered owner of a bar in Barangay Balibago and four others on human-trafficking charges after a 19 May 2025 referral from Destiny Rescue Pilipinas; an entrapment and rescue operation on 1 June 2025 recorded 'barfine' transactions of 5,000 to 10,000 pesos and freed 45 victims, 13 of them minors, who were turned over to the social welfare agency.

In a separate case, the same office arrested a foreign national and accomplices in Angeles City in March 2025 under the Expanded Anti-Trafficking in Persons Act of 2022 (RA 11862) and the child-protection statute RA 7610, after a complaint that women were recruited as Korea-bound performers as cover for work at an Angeles City club. A rescue operation freed 12 victims, five of them minors, and the arrested were presented for inquest before the Office of the City Prosecutor of Angeles City.

Reporting from Angeles City describes hundreds of girls supplied each year to meet demand from foreign men paying for sex, in the city that hosted a former United States military base. More than 150 women and girls told interviewers they wanted to leave prostitution but did not know how. City-regulated entertainers must take weekly STD tests, a requirement activists criticised as marketing the sex industry as clean, and advocates warned that a new airport terminal on the city's outskirts could triple visitor numbers and expand sex trafficking.
localsOnly:
Bataan's SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinance is the region's only recorded local protection for trans residents. Its terms and its enforcement record are not in the source inventory.

For residents working in Angeles City's entertainment sector, city regulation requires registered entertainers to undergo weekly STD testing. Activists quoted in the reporting criticised the requirement as presenting the industry as clean rather than protecting the workers subject to it.

Anti-trafficking operations in Angeles City removed 45 people, 13 of them minors, from commercial sexual exploitation in June 2025, and 12 people, five of them minors, in March 2025, placing them with the social welfare agency. The reporting records that more than 150 women and girls interviewed in the city wanted to leave prostitution and did not know how.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory records a trans-specific killing, assault, prosecution, refusal of service or official action in Central Luzon. Whether the region's provinces and cities enforce the protections that exist, and how, is not sourced.

The Angeles City trafficking cases and the sex-industry reporting are not disaggregated by gender identity or sexual orientation, so they cannot be read as evidence of risk to trans people specifically.

Bataan's SOGIE ordinance is recorded only as existing; its scope, penalties and enforcement are not in the inventory.
